newsitem.title: USA: Reputed mob chief ordered held in Miami jail.
newsitem.headline: Reputed mob chief ordered held in Miami jail.

text.p: Nicholas "Little Nick" Corozzo, the alleged head of New York's Gambino crime family, traded his bathing suit for prison blues and was ordered held in jail Thursday pending an arraignment and bail hearing.

Corozzo, arrested on racketeering charges Wednesday as he sunbathed on a south Florida beach and taken into custody wearing only his swim trunks, made his first appearance in a Miami federal courtroom, where his formal arraignment and bond hearing were postponed until Monday.

Corozzo, 56, and eight "members and associates" of the Gambino family were indicted by a federal grand jury on charges they ran a criminal enterprise called the South Florida Crew, a branch of the Gambino family involved in loansharking and stolen property, prosecutors said.
Joseph Corozzo, Nicholas Corozzo's nephew and lawyer, complained Thursday that his uncle was being held in solitary confinement and denied that the reputed mob boss was involved in loansharking.
"Absolutely false. And I'll prove it in court," he said.
Miami U.S. Attorney William Keefer Wednesday called Corozzo "an alleged captain and currently the ruling member of the Gambino crime family."
The New York Daily News reported that reputed Gambino chieftain John Gotti, jailed for life, had agreed to turn over the reins of the Gambino family to Corozzo to avert a mob war.

Corozzo, wearing glasses, dressed in standard-issue prison blues and sandals and taken into court shackled to other prisoners, chatted casually with co-defendant Ralph Davino as he sat in the prisoner's dock.

Corozzo, 56, Davino, 53, and another alleged Gambino associate, Salvatore Pecchio, 42, stood before U.S. Magistrate Stephen Brown and answered brief questions about whether they understood their rights.
The three were granted adjournments until Monday to give their lawyers time to prepare arguments for bail. Prosecutors asked that the trio be held without bond until trial.

Joseph Corozzo told the court his uncle was in solitary confinement and asked that he be "treated like any other prisoner" at the Miami federal jail where he was held. Brown said he would leave the decision to prison officials.
A 20-count indictment alleged the group was running a loansharking operation from a business called E-Z Check Cashing Inc. in Deerfield Beach, Florida.

The indictment also accused some of the defendants of trying to torch a print shop and conspiring to murder an associate suspected by the Gambino family of skimming money from its south Florida operations.
"There is no substantive count of Nicholas Corozzo attempting to murder anyone," Joseph Corozzo said.
He said his uncle was gainfully employed in the landscaping business and had other "professionals" among members of his family.
Joseph Corozzo acknowledged that his uncle knew John Gotti. He said the two were schoolmates in the 1940s and '50s, but said Nicholas Corozzo had not seen Gotti for some time.
"Certain law enforcement officials allege that he runs the Gambino crime family. Other law enforcement officials say he does not," he said. "The government is conflicted on this."
The defendants faced sentences of 20 years in prison and fines of up to $250,000 on each count, prosecutors said.
